package_info.why_malicious: The affected versions of nghttp2 (and similar HTTP/2 libraries) are vulnerable to a denial-of-service (DoS) attack due to improper handling of HTTP/2 CONTINUATION frames. Attackers can exploit this by sending an excessive number of CONTINUATION frames in a single stream, causing uncontrolled resource consumption and potentially crashing the server. This is a vulnerability, not intentionally malicious code, but it enables malicious exploitation by allowing remote attackers to trigger a DoS condition.

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, when the server receives and processes HTTP/2 traffic from a client connection
execution_context.file_location: Core HTTP/2 frame parsing logic (e.g., nghttp2 library core, http2.c, or equivalent frame handling source file)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, upon receiving HTTP/2 traffic, the code enters a loop to process CONTINUATION frames, appending each frame's payload to a header block without enforcing a maximum frame count or size, resulting in unbounded memory allocation and potential server resource exhaustion.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This logic is suspicious because it allows a remote client to send an unlimited number of CONTINUATION frames, causing the server to allocate memory and CPU resources without restriction, which can be exploited to trigger a denial-of-service condition.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Standard HTTP/2 implementations are expected to enforce strict limits on the number and total size of CONTINUATION frames per stream to prevent resource exhaustion. The vulnerable code fails to enforce such limits, violating protocol robustness and security best practices.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate HTTP/2 clients may use CONTINUATION frames to transmit large header blocks, but the number of frames is always bounded by practical header size limits and protocol constraints; unbounded use is never legitimate.
key_indicators: Absence of a maximum limit on CONTINUATION frame count per stream
No checks on cumulative header block size during frame assembly
Unrestricted memory allocation in header block processing loop
Lack of error handling or connection termination when excessive CONTINUATION frames are received

attack_chain.action: Attacker establishes a single HTTP/2 connection to the vulnerable server.
Attacker sends a HEADERS frame followed by a flood of CONTINUATION frames within the same stream, far exceeding normal usage.
Server's HTTP/2 implementation processes all CONTINUATION frames without limit, consuming excessive memory and CPU resources.
Server performance degrades or the process crashes, resulting in denial of service.

behavioral_signatures: Unusually high number of HTTP/2 CONTINUATION frames in a single stream from a client
Single client connection rapidly consuming server memory and CPU resources
HTTP/2 header block assembly routines lacking frame count or size enforcement
file_indicators: No direct file indicators; detection relies on runtime behavior and server logs
Abnormally high or rapidly increasing memory usage by HTTP/2 server processes (e.g., nghttp2, httpd, nginx, etc.)
network_indicators: HTTP/2 streams containing hundreds or thousands of CONTINUATION frames from a single client IP
Abnormal HTTP/2 traffic patterns with header blocks split into excessive numbers of CONTINUATION frames
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor HTTP/2 traffic for streams with an excessive number of CONTINUATION frames per stream or per connection. Set and enforce thresholds for the maximum allowed CONTINUATION frames and header block sizes. Correlate spikes in server resource usage with HTTP/2 traffic patterns. Analyze server logs for repeated or unusually large header block assembly events. Deploy WAF or IDS/IPS rules to detect and block HTTP/2 frame floods. Patch affected HTTP/2 libraries to enforce strict protocol limits and reject abusive streams.
